claims.text: Adding a small amount of Hf to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance.
High-temperature oxidation of the Hf-modified alloy will form a protective oxide layer.
The proposed protective oxide layer can be formed by exposure to air at 1000 °C for 100 hours.
The resulting oxide layer will prevent or suppress further oxidation.
Adding a small amount of Hf can enhance mechanical properties without significantly reducing ductility.
Hf enhances the mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr through solid-solution strengthening.
The proposed intervention will improve oxidation resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance.
The treated alloy will have a yield strength of 200–500 MPa at 1000 °C.
The treated alloy will retain room-temperature tensile ductility of 8–16%.
The mechanical-performance prediction applies to tensile loading at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The central claim requires oxidation improvement without sacrificing mechanical performance, whereas the falsification rule requires both oxidation resistance and mechanical properties to improve. Retaining baseline mechanical performance and improving it are different criteria.

The stated mechanical mechanism is solid-solution strengthening, but both cited records attribute Hf-related strengthening in CoCrFeNi alloys to precipitation of intermetallic Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases.
